\title{\textbf{Multi-Agent Validator System}\\
Independent Evidence for Scientific Claim Verification}
\author{}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
False endorsement is a costly error in scientific claim checking. We test
whether searching beyond the supplied citations reduces it. The validator
stages four isolated roles over two
evidence scopes: a sealed reader that answers a neutral question from
retrieved passages before seeing the claim, a claim-visible judge over four
labels (supported, contradicted, unaddressed, underdetermined), a citation
auditor over the original references, and a reconciler that reports the two
scopes separately instead of collapsing them into one score. Every stage fails
closed: a transport or parse failure is an execution status, never a
scientific verdict.

On SciFact, we compare the system with a baseline that already reads the
original citations. Across 300 development claims, the baseline incorrectly
endorses about 1 in 100 claims whose gold label is not support; the staged
validator makes no such endorsement. Yet it finds only 43\% of supported
claims, compared with 57\% for the baseline. A separate 300-claim held-out
sample shows the same trade-off, with 38 validator requests failing closed.
The reduction is \emph{not statistically significant}. We replicate the
comparison with a MiniMax family and on a frozen thirty-claim subset with
\sweepModelsWord{} models, \sweepSplit{}. The direction is stable: false
endorsement never rises, and the cost appears as withheld contradictions.
Disagreement between evidence scopes drives many abstentions. In this benchmark, every annotated gold
document is already among the cited documents, limiting what independent
retrieval can add. We report the negative result with a mechanism analysis
and cost accounting. The system offers more conservative verdicts, but
misses more supported claims.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Artifact.} All tables and figures in this paper are generated
from saved prediction files by the scripts in \texttt{scripts/paper/}. The
corpus, splits, prompts, and frozen configurations are in the accompanying
repository, and the held-out split is protected by a hash freeze that
refuses a run whose model, prompt, configuration, or corpus differs from the
locked record.

\section{Introduction}

Large language models are now asked to check claims, not only to make them.
In the usual pipeline a checker sees a claim and the citations offered with
it, then returns a verdict. It therefore inherits the generator's evidence:
if the generator cited the wrong paper, or cited a paper that supports a
slightly different claim, the checker reads the same biased evidence set and
cannot notice. The failure is a property of the information it is given, not a
bug in the checker.

One remedy is to have the checker search for its own evidence. Recent work in
retrieval-augmented factuality evaluation \citep{wei2024longform}, in
self-check agents \citep{march2026,hirsch2026blame}, and in
retrieval-augmented verifiers \citep{yue2024rafts,zheng2024rav} points in
that direction. Independent retrieval plus careful staging is widely assumed
to help. It has rarely been tested against a strong same-evidence baseline on
scientific claims, where the original citations are often correct and where
an abstention can be the right answer.

This paper tests the assumption directly. We build a staged validator
(\textbf{V}) that separates four roles (a sealed evidence reader, a
claim-visible judge, a citation auditor, and a reconciler) over two evidence
scopes: the original citations (\Dzero) and independently retrieved abstracts
(\Done). We compare it against a same-evidence baseline (\textbf{B2}) that
reads a neutral question over the original citations in an isolated reader and
then compares, which is the strongest same-evidence configuration we could
build without training. We also build the full factorial around the two
interventions we care about: evidence access (\Dzero{} versus \Done) and
reading policy (claim-visible versus neutral-question evidence-first).

Our preregistered primary outcome is false endorsement: the rate at which a
method predicts ``supported'' for a claim that the gold labels do not
support. The observed answer is inconclusive. On the frozen development sample the
paired difference between V and B2 is \lunadevfediff{} with a 95\% interval of
\lunadevfeci{}, which includes zero. The held-out sample repeats the pattern.
The staged validator does reach zero false endorsements, but it buys that by
withholding support: SUPPORT recall drops from \lunadevBTwosupportRecall{} to
\lunadevVsupportRecall{} on the development sample, and on the held-out
sample \lunaheldVfailclosed{} of 300 claims fail closed entirely. Both
false endorsement and support recall are needed to judge the trade-off.

Three findings frame the result.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Independent retrieval is not the bottleneck; scope
    reconciliation is.} The failure analysis shows that the dominant mode of
  V is not a retrieval miss but a disagreement between the D0 and D1
  judgments, which the reconciler resolves conservatively into
  ``underdetermined''. When the two scopes agree, V inherits the baseline's
  accuracy; when they disagree, V abstains. In practice the system behaves as
  a disagreement detector.
  \item \textbf{Staged judgment buys precision, not overall accuracy.}
  Micro-F1 falls because recall falls faster than precision rises.
  Reported as F1 alone, this looks like a regression (\lunadevBTwomicroFOne{}
  against \lunadevVmicroFOne{}); reported as a precision--coverage trade-off it
  is a usable operating point for a conservative reader-facing tool.
  \item \textbf{The direction repeats across models.} We repeat the pairing
  on a fixed thirty-claim subset with \sweepModelsWord{} instruction-tuned
  models, \sweepSplit{}. False endorsement never rises under staging, and the
  cost lands on contradiction rather than on support: REFUTE recall falls in
  \sweepRefuteLowerPhrase{} while SUPPORT recall barely moves. The subset is small, so this is a statement about direction,
  not significance.
\end{itemize}

No human study was run: no participant was recruited, no ethics review was
obtained, and we make no claim about human trust. The four-way labels are
described but not scored, because SciFact's label space is three-way and has
no annotation for the distinction. The baselines are prompt-level adaptations
of the named mechanisms, not reproductions of trained verifiers. Finally, our
corpus is a fixed set of biomedical abstracts, so every claim of support is
relative to that corpus and retrieval budget.

The contribution is a reproducible negative result with a mechanism rather
than a new score: a measurement of what independent retrieval and
evidence-first staging do, and do not do, to a scientific claim checker,
together with the artifact that makes it checkable.

\section{Related Work}

\subsection{Verification datasets and scientific claim checking}

FEVER \citep{thorne2018fever} established the claim--evidence verification
format that this paper follows, and FEVEROUS \citep{aly2021feverous} extended
it to unstructured and structured evidence. SciFact \citep{wadden2020scifact}
is the benchmark used here: it pairs scientific claims with abstracts and
rationale sentences, and supplies support, refute, and
insufficient-information labels. SciFact-Open \citep{wadden2022scifactopen}
extends the task to open-domain retrieval, which motivates our separation of
a frozen corpus from live search; we use a frozen corpus only, and we do not
claim open-domain performance. Missci \citep{glockner2024missci} targets
misrepresented science and fallacy reconstruction rather than four-way claim
labeling, and RAGTruth \citep{niu2024ragtruth} targets context faithfulness
of retrieval-augmented generation rather than evidence sufficiency of a
checker; we cite both as boundaries of our setting rather than as
benchmarks we score. For biomedical claims specifically, SciClaims
\citep{ortega2025sciclaims} provides an end-to-end generative pipeline; we
treat it as prior art for scientific verification with explanations and do not
reproduce it. Vladika and Matthes \citep{vladika2024knowledge} compare
knowledge sources for open-domain scientific claim verification and motivate
our interest in whether a different evidence source changes verdicts.

\subsection{LLM verifiers, self-checking agents, and retrieval}

A long line of work asks an LLM to judge claims. Chain-of-Verification
\citep{dhuliawala2024cove} isolates the verification questions from the draft
answer, which is the closest published analogue to our information separation
and which our B2 baseline deliberately imitates. Safe \citep{wei2024longform}
verifies atomic facts with search and is the reference point for our fresh
retrieval arm. Self-checking agents such as MARCH
\citep{march2026,march2026code} add information separation between proposer
and checker, and blame-localization work \citep{hirsch2026blame} shows that
trace-level attribution of citation errors is a developer-facing diagnostic
distinct from evaluating a final conclusion for an end user; we evaluate final
conclusions, and cite the trace work as the reason not to claim it. A
systematic auditor for retrieval-augmented generation \citep{yu2026rt4chart}
and retrieval-augmented verifiers such as RAFTS \citep{yue2024rafts} and RAV
\citep{zheng2024rav} further motivate separating evidence discovery from
judgment. Explainable fact checking through question answering
\citep{yang2022explainablefactchecking} and hallucination detection methods
such as SelfCheckGPT \citep{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} and RARR
\citep{gao2023rarr} address the neighbouring problem of detecting unsupported
content in model output.

Little in the design is new in isolation. Atomic decomposition, blinded
checking, search-based verification, and readable explanations each have
substantial prior art. Our contribution is a controlled measurement of their
combination against a strong same-evidence control, and a negative result
about that combination.

\subsection{Abstention, calibration, and selective use}

A checker that cannot abstain will answer when it should not. Work on
abstention \citep{feng2024abstain} and on calibrated selective fact checking
\citep{yang2026calibratedselective} formalises the trade-off we measure.
Calibration theory \citep{guo2017calibration} distinguishes a model's
verbalised confidence from a probability fitted on held-out data; we fit a
single temperature on a calibration split and report raw and calibrated
numbers separately. Because a scientific ``underdetermined'' verdict and a
system-level ``defer to a reviewer'' action are different things, we keep them
in separate fields. On the human side, confidence and explanation are known to
affect both accuracy and trust calibration in AI-assisted decisions
\citep{zhang2020trustcalibration}, so we do not claim that human trust
calibration is unstudied; we did not run the study and we report the
protocol without results.

\section{Problem Formulation}

\subsection{Inputs and evidence scopes}

Let $c$ be an atomic scientific claim taken from a frozen report. A claim
carries an exact source span, a normalised statement, and a \emph{neutral
question}: a single interrogative formulation of the claim that preserves
population, comparator, units, and causal scope but does not contain the
asserted answer. Two evidence scopes are available:

\begin{itemize}
  \item $\Dzero$ --- the documents the original report cited. These are the
    generator's evidence. A judgment over $\Dzero$ answers: \emph{is the
    original citation set faithful to the claim?}
  \item $\Done$ --- documents retrieved independently from a frozen corpus
    using the neutral question, with the claim's answer, the report, and
    $\Dzero$ hidden from the retrieval and reading stages. A judgment over
    $\Done$ answers: \emph{what does independent retrieval establish?}
\end{itemize}

A verdict is always relative to a stated scope, corpus, and search budget. It
is not an unrestricted declaration of scientific truth. The reconciled
judgment over $\Dunion$ answers: \emph{what can be said once both scopes are
considered?}

\subsection{Four labels}

Internally the system uses four labels, defined relative to a specified
evidence collection:

\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.1em,style=nextline]
  \item[Supported] Relevant evidence establishes the exact scoped assertion
    and no unresolved material counterevidence remains in the reviewed pool.
  \item[Contradicted] Relevant evidence establishes an incompatible
    assertion; apparent conflicts have been resolved by scope or relevance.
  \item[Unaddressed] No reviewed relevant passage answers the claim under
    the stated corpus and retrieval budget.
  \item[Underdetermined] Relevant evidence exists, but disagreement,
    imprecision, incomplete measurement, or an unsupported inference prevents
    resolution.
\end{description}

The decision order is: check execution status and claim validity; then
assess relevance; if no passage addresses the claim, use \emph{unaddressed};
if relevant evidence is materially conflicting or inconclusive, use
\emph{underdetermined}; otherwise apply support or contradiction, but only at
the preserved scope. A non-significant result is not automatically proof of
no effect, and a null-result claim requires its own evidence assessment.

SciFact's native label space is three-way, so the scored mapping is
supported $\to$ SUPPORT, contradicted $\to$ REFUTE, and unaddressed or
underdetermined $\to$ NEI. The four-way distinction is therefore
\emph{reported but not scored} against gold. We say this once here and repeat
it wherever a number could be misread.

\subsection{Research questions}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{RQ1 (primary, preregistered).} At a matched inference
    budget, does independent retrieval plus staged evidence-first judgment
    reduce false endorsement relative to same-evidence checking?
  \item \textbf{RQ2 (descriptive).} Can the system distinguish missing
    evidence from unresolved evidence, and how often does it defer?
  \item \textbf{RQ3 (deferred).} Do evidence-linked explanations improve
    non-experts' judgments, including when the validator is wrong? No
    participant was recruited; Appendix~\ref{app:human-study} gives the
    protocol and no results.
  \item \textbf{RQ4 (secondary).} How do accuracy, coverage, latency, and
    cost change across generator/checker families and across the two
    interventions?
\end{itemize}

\section{System Design}

Figure~\ref{fig:architecture} shows the staged pipeline and its information
boundaries. Roles are isolated functions with typed inputs; several roles may
call the same underlying model in separate stateless requests. Separate
roles do not imply statistically independent errors, so we measure
model-family dependence rather than assume it.

\subsection{Roles and information boundaries}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{The validation procedure for one claim. ``Scope'' is the evidence
collection a step may read; no step may read outside its scope. A failure in
any step produces an execution status and stops the claim.}
\label{tab:pipeline}
\begin{tabular}{rlll}
\toprule
Step & Role & Reads & Writes \\
\midrule
1 & Proposer & report & atomic claims, neutral questions \\
2 & Gatherer & neutral question, corpus & $D_1$ passages \\
3 & Reader & neutral question, $D_1$ & sealed evidence record \\
4 & Judge & claim, sealed record, $D_1$ & four-way label, spans \\
5 & Auditor & claim, $D_0$ & $D_0$ label, citation adequacy \\
6 & Reconciler & steps 4 and 5 & reconciled label, conflicts \\
7 & Renderer & reconciled record & claim card \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.1em,style=nextline]
  \item[Proposer.] Maps a report to atomic claims, neutral questions, asserted
    answers, and exact source spans. Quantities, confidence language,
    population, comparator, and causal scope are preserved; a conjunction is
    split while the relation between its parts is retained.
  \item[Independent gatherer.] Given the neutral question, a scope, and the
    corpus, retrieves fresh evidence. The asserted answer, the report, the
    original citations, and the generator's identity are hidden. Three query
    forms are issued per claim (open inquiry; scope and measurement;
    limitations or null results); the top candidates are deduplicated and
    reranked, and up to eight passages are kept.
  \item[Evidence reader.] Answers the neutral question from the shuffled
    retrieved passages and cites the passage identifiers it used. Its record
    is \emph{sealed} before the claim is revealed.
  \item[Judge.] Sees the atomic claim, the sealed reader record, and the
    evidence passages, and assigns one of the four labels together with
    rationale codes, cited spans, and uncertainty reasons.
  \item[Citation auditor.] Judges the claim against $\Dzero$ alone and rates
    each citation's adequacy. It never sees $\Done$.
  \item[Reconciler.] Combines the two judgments, explains the difference,
    and flags invalid inference links between claims.
  \item[Renderer.] Produces plain-language claim cards from the validated
    structured record only. It introduces no new factual claims.
\end{description}

The blinding is partial: a neutral question still reveals the topic and may
leak assumptions. The isolation guarantee is structural, not semantic. The
reader's payload contains only the neutral question and passage text, and an
assertion on the payload shape plus a test suite enforce that.

\subsection{Execution and stopping}

The report is generated once and frozen. Validation does not rewrite it. A
claim budget of eight claims per report, two retrieval rounds, three query
forms per round, and eight passages in the judge context are development
defaults that were frozen before the held-out run. A second retrieval round
is permitted only for unresolved questions, scope mismatch, or contradictory
evidence; a run stops on exhausted budget, no new eligible documents, or a
complete bounded evidence record. Every intermediate artifact is persisted,
and the runner resumes at the last completed claim without mixing
configurations.

The system fails closed by default. When the model
returns malformed JSON, cites a passage it was not given, or the endpoint
fails, the system records an execution status of \texttt{failed} or
\texttt{timeout} and a placeholder label that is a schema token, never model
text. These rows are excluded from scored metrics and reported separately.
They are never silently remapped into a scientific verdict.

\subsection{Reconciliation}

Agreement between scopes copies the shared label. A disagreement, or a failed
D0 audit, resolves to \emph{underdetermined} and hence to NEI on the scored
label space. We do not repair citation faithfulness with outside evidence: a
claim can be unsupported by its own citation and supported elsewhere, and the
two facts are reported separately.

\section{Implementation}

\subsection{Records and reproducibility contract}

The implementation emits a machine-readable prediction file and an immutable
run sidecar for every condition. The run record carries a run identifier,
split, seed, model identifier and revision, prompt-bundle hash, corpus hash,
configuration hash, timestamps, token totals, and an execution status; the
sidecar adds the prompt files and their individual hashes. Predictions carry
the claim identifier, the predicted label, the four-way label where
applicable, the evidence scope, the rationale codes, and the execution
status. Schema validation is enforced before a file is accepted.

The corpus is frozen by a SHA-256 hash over the canonicalised abstract
corpus, and the split manifests are locked separately. The held-out split is
protected by a freeze record containing the model identifier, the corpus
hash, and per-method configuration and prompt hashes; a held-out run refuses
to start unless the observed hashes match the frozen ones. This is what
makes ``we ran the held-out split once'' a checkable statement rather than
an assurance.

\subsection{Retrieval}

Retrieval is BM25 (Okapi, $k_1=1.5$, $b=0.75$, epsilon idf floor)
implemented in pure Python over the frozen abstract corpus, with a fixed
alphanumeric lower-case tokenizer and no stemming. For each neutral question
three query templates are used; the top 20 candidates per query are merged,
deduplicated, and reranked by maximum BM25 score, and at most eight passages
are passed to the judge. Adjacent sentences of one document are kept
together where needed to resolve negation or units. Dense retrieval and
reciprocal-rank fusion were prepared but are not enabled in the product path;
they are development-time comparisons, and we do not report a dense
retrieval result we did not measure.

\subsection{Models and harness}

We evaluate two model families on the full samples to satisfy RQ4 and to
protect the negative result from being an artefact of one model's behaviour,
and we repeat the pairing on a wider set of models over the fixed subset of
Section~\ref{sec:sweep}.

\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.1em,style=nextline]
  \item[\textsc{GPT-6 Luna}.] A hosted instruction-tuned model accessed
    through an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint. It is the model behind the
    powered comparison, the held-out run, and the cost accounting.
  \item[\textsc{MiniMax M3.1 Flash}.] A second, architecturally unrelated
    instruction-tuned model, accessed through the local agent runtime. To
    keep the repository's endpoint policy intact we expose that runtime
    through a small loopback bridge that implements the OpenAI chat
    completions interface, one fresh session per request. A fresh session
    per request matters: a shared session would carry earlier claims into
    later ones and break the information-isolation guarantee the validator is
    measured on. The harness adds a fixed agent preamble and tool
    definitions to every request; the preamble is byte-identical across
    conditions, so it cancels in every comparison, but it inflates the
    prompt-token counts. That is why cost is reported for the Luna family
    only, and why the MiniMax family contributes no cost row.
  \item[\textsc{Wider set}.] The sweep adds \sweepAdditionalWord{} more models
    on that subset: \sweepAdditionalList{}. \sweepRoute{}
\end{description}

All models run with temperature $0$ where the endpoint accepts it, and with
the same prompts, frozen corpus, claim sample, and budgets. The prompts are
versioned text files under \texttt{prompts/}; their hashes enter the freeze
record.

\subsection{Failure handling and the retry policy}

Three different things can go wrong, and the paper keeps them apart.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Transport failure.} The endpoint refuses the connection or
    returns a retryable status. The client retries with exponential backoff.
  \item \textbf{Protocol failure.} The model returns text that is not the
    requested JSON, cites a passage it was not given, or returns a label
    outside the allowed set. The parser rejects it. This is a
    \emph{parse} failure, not a scientific disagreement.
  \item \textbf{Scope conflict.} Both stages completed and disagree. This is
    a scientific outcome: the reconciled verdict is
    \emph{underdetermined}, which maps to NEI.
\end{enumerate}

The first two produce an execution status of \texttt{failed} and are
excluded from the scored metrics; the third is scored normally. Because a
failed request is not evidence about the claim, the runner retries it, up to
four attempts per claim, and drops the failed row from the prediction file
between attempts so that the resume re-claims exactly those claims. The
policy is applied identically to every condition and every model family on
the development sample.

Because dropping failed rows could flatter a method that fails on the hard
claims, we report a second, stricter accounting in which every submitted row
is scored with the label the method recorded for it. On the fail-closed
paths that label is the conservative NEI, so the strict accounting can only
hurt a method. Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity} shows that the primary comparison
does not depend on the choice.

One asymmetry remains: the held-out run was always planned as a single
execution and does not use the retry policy, so its fail-closed count includes
unrecovered execution failures.

\subsection{Prompt contracts}

Each role has a fixed output contract, expressed in the prompt and enforced
by the parser. The reader must return an answer and the identifiers of the
passages it used; the judge must return one of four labels, rationale codes,
cited span identifiers, and uncertainty reasons; the citation auditor must
return a label plus a per-citation adequacy rating from
\{adequate, inadequate, unverifiable\} and a defect list. The parsers reject
a label outside the allowed set, a cited identifier that was not supplied,
and any missing field. Appendix~\ref{app:prompts} states each contract; the
prompt text itself is in the repository, versioned and hashed.

\section{Experimental Setup}

\subsection{Data and splits}

We use SciFact \citep{wadden2020scifact}. The corpus is the released set of
biomedical abstracts, frozen by hash. The released training claims are split
into a calibration subset of 100 claims, reserved before any prompt work,
and a development pool of 709 claims. The public development split (300
claims) is used as a \emph{local} held-out evaluation set; it is not an
untouched community test set, and we name it accordingly throughout. Official
test labels are not used.

Two samples are frozen by manifest: a 300-claim development sample drawn with
a fixed seed from the training pool (\texttt{dev300\_seed42.json} under
\texttt{data/manifests/}), used for all development and prompt decisions, and
a 300-claim evaluation sample consisting of SciFact's public development
split, held out locally and used once under the freeze record. Both samples
group claims by cited-document family so that paraphrases and derivative
claims do not straddle the comparison.

\subsection{Conditions}

All conditions share the frozen reports, the corpus snapshot, the claim
sample, the scoring code, and the prompt files. They differ only in the
intervention named in the table.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{The condition matrix. ``Adaptation'' means a prompt-level
implementation of the named mechanism, never a reproduction of a trained
system. The 2$\times$2 factorial is B1/B2 (evidence $\Dzero$) against
B3/V-D1 (evidence $\Done$), crossed with claim-visible against
neutral-question evidence-first reading.}
\label{tab:conditions}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
ID & Condition & Evidence and reading policy \\
\midrule
B0 & Prior-knowledge judge & No evidence; claim only \\
B1 & Atomic claim, claim-visible judge & $\Dzero$; claim-visible \\
B2 & Neutral question, isolated reader, compare & $\Dzero$; evidence-first \\
B3 & Fresh retrieval, direct judge & $\Done$; claim-visible \\
V-D1 & Fresh retrieval, isolated reader, judge & $\Done$; evidence-first \\
V & Full staged validator & $\Dunion$; reconciled \\
O & Evidence oracle (diagnostic) & Gold rationale sentences \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

B0 measures how much the model answers from parametric knowledge alone and
acts as a floor. O supplies the gold rationale sentences to the same
claim-visible judge and is a diagnostic ceiling, not a deployable competitor.
V-D1 is the D1 arm of V, recovered from the V predictions by a mapping step
rather than a second model run, so it inherits V's failure modes by
construction.

\subsection{Metrics}

Verification quality is measured by per-class precision, recall and F1, plus
micro and macro F1 on the native three-way label space. The primary metric
is \emph{false endorsement}: the number of claims predicted SUPPORT whose
gold label is not support, divided by the number of gold non-support claims.
We report the second denominator (false endorsements over all predicted
SUPPORT claims) as well, because the two answer different questions.
Coverage is the fraction of submitted claims that produced a scored
prediction; fail-closed rows are counted and reported, never dropped
silently. Calibration is measured with multiclass Brier score, negative
log-likelihood, and expected calibration error, fitted with a single
temperature on the calibration split only. Cost is reported as calls per
claim, measured tokens per call, and per-call latency, because a resumed run
keeps only its last invocation's usage record and per-claim token totals are
therefore not recoverable.

\subsection{Statistics and preregistration}

One primary comparison was preregistered before the held-out run: V versus
B2 on false endorsement with the gold non-support denominator. The interval
is a paired cluster bootstrap over cited-document families, 2000 resamples,
95\% percentile interval; a claim enters the comparison only when every
compared method produced an execution-ok, gold-labelled row, and dropped
claims are counted. Secondary comparisons within a declared family are
Holm-adjusted; everything else is labelled exploratory. The factorial
comparison is used to interpret the mechanism, not to claim additional
significance.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Primary comparison}

Table~\ref{tab:main-dev} gives the development results and
Table~\ref{tab:paired-dev} the preregistered paired comparison. In the API
family, B2 reaches micro-F1 \lunadevBTwomicroFOne{} with false endorsement
\lunadevBTwofe{}, while V reaches micro-F1 \lunadevVmicroFOne{} with false
endorsement \lunadevVfe{} on all \lunadevVn{} scored claims. The paired
difference in false endorsement is \lunadevfediff{} with 95\% interval
\lunadevfeci{} over \lunadevnpaired{} paired claims and \lunadevnfamilies{}
families: the interval includes zero, so the primary comparison is null. The
MiniMax family behaves the same way: B2 reaches micro-F1
\mmdevBTwomicroFOne{} with false endorsement \mmdevBTwofe{}, V reaches
\mmdevVmicroFOne{} with \mmdevVfe{}, and the paired difference is
\mmdevfediff{} (\mmdevfeci{}) over \mmdevnpaired{} paired claims, again
including zero.

Fail-closed rows are excluded from the scored metrics above, so a method
could in principle look better by failing on the hard claims. Table
\ref{tab:sensitivity} therefore repeats the two primary conditions under
both accountings. Under the all-rows accounting every submitted claim is
scored with the label the method recorded for it, which is the conservative
NEI on every fail-closed path in this repository. The comparison does not
depend on the choice: V's false endorsement is zero under both accountings
on the development sample, where the retry policy recovered every failed
request. On the held-out sample, which ran once without that policy, the
all-rows accounting lowers V's micro-F1 from \lunaheldVmicroFOne{} to
\lunaheldVallrowsmicroFOne{} while its false endorsement stays at zero.

The held-out sample reproduces the pattern. B2 reaches micro-F1
\lunaheldBTwomicroFOne{} with false endorsement \lunaheldBTwofe{}, and V reaches
micro-F1 \lunaheldVmicroFOne{} with false endorsement \lunaheldVfe{} on
\lunaheldVn{} scored claims with \lunaheldVfailclosed{} failures. The paired
difference is \lunaheldfediff{} (\lunaheldfeci{}), again including zero.

The null has structure. V achieves near-perfect precision on the endorsement
class (SUPPORT precision \lunadevVsupportPrecision{} in the Luna family,
\mmdevVsupportPrecision{} in the second) and pays for it in recall. The
system is a conservative checker, not a better one. Micro-F1 alone reads as a
regression, and false endorsement alone reads as a success; the paired
interval is what distinguishes the two readings.

\subsection{The 2$\times$2 factorial}

Table~\ref{tab:ablation} separates the two interventions.
\textbf{Evidence access} is the row difference (B1 versus B3, and B2 versus
V-D1); \textbf{reading policy} is the column difference (B1 versus B2, and
B3 versus V-D1). The table shows three effects.

First, \emph{claim-visible judging beats evidence-first judging} on the
scored label space: B1 (D0, claim-visible) beats B2 (D0, evidence-first) on
micro-F1 (\lunadevBOnemicroFOne{} versus \lunadevBTwomicroFOne{}), and B3 (D1,
claim-visible) beats V-D1 (D1, evidence-first) (\lunadevBThreemicroFOne{} versus
\lunadevVDOnemicroFOne{}). This is the opposite of the intuition behind
evidence-first staging. Reading the evidence without the claim in view loses
information that the judge needs; the sealing buys isolation, not accuracy.

Second, \emph{evidence access barely moves the evidence-first cell}: V-D1's
false endorsement (\lunadevVDOnefe{}) is close to B2's (\lunadevBTwofe{}) even
though V-D1 has access to a larger evidence pool, and in the MiniMax family
the two are equal (\mmdevVDOnefe{} against \mmdevBTwofe{}). Independent
retrieval introduces documents that the original claim was never calibrated
against, and it does not buy accuracy.

Third, \emph{the full V is more conservative than either arm}, because the
reconciler resolves scope disagreement into abstention rather than choosing
a side. V's zero false endorsement is thus a property of the reconciliation
policy, not of the retrieval.

The factorial is a Luna-family result. The MiniMax family contributes only
B1, B2, V-D1 and V, and those rows do not repeat the claim-visible
advantage: there B1 reaches micro-F1 \mmdevBOnemicroFOne{} against B2's
\mmdevBTwomicroFOne{}, and B1 is the less conservative arm (false endorsement
\mmdevBOnefe{} against \mmdevBTwofe{}). We therefore state the factorial as a
finding about this benchmark under one model family, and treat its
replication as open rather than asserting it.

\end{table}

\mmdevBTwosupportRecall{} against \mmdevVsupportRecall{}) and with lower NEI

far more claims and many of those claims are supported.

\subsection{Model-family transfer}

Table~\ref{tab:main-dev} reports both families. The pattern (V more
conservative than B2, lower SUPPORT recall, false endorsement at or near
zero, primary interval including zero) is reproduced under a second model
family reached through a different harness: the paired false-endorsement
difference is \lunadevfediff{} (\lunadevfeci{}) for the Luna family and
\mmdevfediff{} (\mmdevfeci{}) for the second. The two families differ in
absolute quality: the MiniMax family is a markedly better verifier on this
benchmark (B2 micro-F1 \mmdevBTwomicroFOne{} against
\lunadevBTwomicroFOne{}), and the direction of the V effect is the same in
both. This is consistent with the staged design producing a conservative
operating point, although two model families cannot establish that as a
general effect. We do not read it as evidence about the absolute quality of either
model; the two families are not matched for size, training data, or
capability, and the comparison is between families of systems, not between
models of equal strength. We also cannot separate the MiniMax family's model
prior from its design: its prior-knowledge condition (B0) and its
claim-visible D1 condition (B3) did not complete before the free endpoint
that served it was withdrawn, so the MiniMax family contributes its B1, B2 and
V rows rather than the full factorial. It corroborates the preregistered
comparison and not the wider factorial.

\subsection{The shift across \sweepModelsWord{} models}
\label{sec:sweep}

Two families answer the preregistered question, but not whether the
conservative shift belongs to the design or to the two models we happened to
run. To check the direction more widely we repeated the same B2-versus-V
pairing on a frozen subset of the development sample: ten SUPPORT, ten
REFUTE, and ten NEI claims, selected with seed~42 before any model was run.
In total \sweepModelsWord{} instruction-tuned models took part,
\sweepSplit{}. All used the same prompts, corpus, retrieval budget, and
scoring code.
Table~\ref{tab:sweep} lists them.

The subset is small and we read it that way. Thirty claims can resolve a
difference of roughly ten percentage points, not the one-point
false-endorsement rate the full sample was sized for. Most of the paired
intervals in Table~\ref{tab:sweep} therefore collapse to a point at zero, and
we do not test these rows for significance. What the subset can show is where
on the label set the conservative shift lands.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{B2 versus V on the frozen thirty-claim subset. Cells after the
interval are ``B2 / V''. $\Delta$FE is the paired difference in false
endorsement with its 95\% interval; a positive value means V endorses more.
The subset is descriptive, not powered: read it for direction, not for
significance.}
\label{tab:sweep}
\input{paper/tables/t10_sweep}
\end{table}

Two regularities hold across the rows. False endorsement never rises:
$\Delta$FE is zero in \sweepEqualWord{} of the \sweepModelsWord{} models,
negative in \sweepLowerWord{}, and positive in \sweepHigherWord{};
\sweepExcludeZeroWord{} of the \sweepModelsWord{} intervals exclude zero. And
the abstention lands on contradiction rather than on support: REFUTE recall is
lower under V in \sweepRefuteLowerWord{} of the \sweepModelsWord{} models and
unchanged in \sweepRefuteEqualWord{}, while SUPPORT recall is unchanged in
\sweepSupportEqualWord{} models and lower in \sweepSupportLowerWord{}.
Micro-F1 falls in \sweepFOneLowerWord{} of the \sweepModelsWord{}.

The closed-weight rows make the pattern visible. Under B2 each of them
identifies most refuted claims; under V each of them identifies half. Support
recall moves by at most one claim in the same rows. On the full sample the
loss is not exclusive to REFUTE (Table~\ref{tab:perclass} shows both classes
falling), so the subset is better read as showing where the shift is
concentrated than as a separate finding. The mechanism is the same one Section~\ref{sec:results-cases}
describes: when the two scopes disagree, the reconciler prefers
\emph{underdetermined}, and disagreement is more common exactly where a
citation states the opposite of the claim.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{paper/figures/model_sweep.pdf}
\caption{B2 to V on the thirty-claim subset, per model. Hollow marks are B2,
filled marks are V. The conservative shift costs REFUTE recall in
\sweepRefuteLowerPhrase{} while SUPPORT recall and false endorsement barely
move; the largest false-endorsement rate in any row is \sweepFEmaxPct{}.}
\label{fig:modelsweep}
\end{figure}

The claim-level records say whether the models lose the same claims or
different ones. Of the \sweepRefuteTotalWord{} refuted claims that the baseline
identifies, \sweepRefuteAllWord{} are withheld under V by every model that
called them refuted, \sweepRefuteNoneWord{} by none, and \sweepRefuteSomeWord{}
by some but not all: the recall loss is a handful of specific claims, not a
diffuse erosion. Support loss is concentrated the same way: of the
\sweepSupportTotalWord{} supported claims the baseline finds,
\sweepSupportNoneWord{} are kept by every model and \sweepSupportSomeWord{} is
lost by some but not all. No model gains a refutation the baseline missed, and
the reverse gain for support occurs in \sweepGainedSupportPhrase{}. The models also agree on the
labels themselves: all \sweepModelsWord{} give the same B2 label on
\sweepAgreeBTwo{} of the thirty claims and the same V label on \sweepAgreeV{}.

The sweep also bounds how much of the result can be a model artefact. Models
differ in absolute quality: B2 micro-F1 ranges from \sweepBTwomin{} to
\sweepBTwomax{} across the \sweepModelsWord{}, and that ordering does not
predict which models lose the most under staging. What does not vary is the
direction of the change. A design whose only effect were to make a weak model
abstain more would not produce that regularity.

\subsection{Where the abstentions come from}

The RQ2 descriptive split is available because V stores its four-way label
alongside the mapped native label. On the development sample V predicts NEI
on \lunadevVlabelsnei{} of \lunadevVlabelstotal{} claims
(\lunadevVlabelsneishare{} of the sample), and those NEI predictions split into
\emph{unaddressed} (no retrieved passage addresses the claim,
\lunadevVlabelsunaddressed{} claims) and \emph{underdetermined} (relevant
evidence exists but does not resolve, \lunadevVlabelsunderdetermined{}
claims). Figure~\ref{fig:labels} shows the distribution.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.62\textwidth]{paper/figures/label_distribution.pdf}
\caption{V's four-way verdicts on the development sample, before the mapping
onto SciFact's three-way label space. The split between \emph{unaddressed}
and \emph{underdetermined} is descriptive: SciFact's gold cannot score it.}
\label{fig:labels}
\end{figure}

Whether the two scopes agreed is more informative than the four-way label. V
records a \texttt{d0\_d1\_conflict} code when the \Dzero{} and \Done{}
four-way verdicts differ, and the reconciler then abstains by construction.
Table~\ref{tab:mechanism} conditions accuracy on that split.
When the scopes agree, V's accuracy matches the baseline's
(\lunadevAgreeBTwosAcc{} against \lunadevAgreeVacc{} on the development
sample); when they differ, V abstains on every claim and its accuracy falls
to the share of NEI in that subset (\lunadevConflictVacc{}). The shape
repeats on the held-out sample (\lunaheldAgreeVacc{} against
\lunaheldAgreeBTwosAcc{} when the scopes agree, \lunaheldConflictVacc{} when
they differ) and in the MiniMax family (\mmdevAgreeVacc{} against
\mmdevAgreeBTwosAcc{}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Accuracy conditioned on whether the two evidence scopes agree.
``Differ'' means the run recorded \texttt{d0\_d1\_conflict}; V abstains on
every such claim by construction, so the column measures how often NEI
happens to be the gold label. Fail-closed rows are excluded.}
\label{tab:mechanism}
\input{paper/tables/t9_mechanism}
\end{table}

Of the \lunadevVlabelsnei{} NEI verdicts,
\lunadevConflictN{} are scope conflicts. The other \lunadevAgreeNeiCount{}
are agreed negatives: \lunadevAgreeUnaddressed{} unaddressed and
\lunadevAgreeUnderdetermined{} underdetermined.

Retrieval is not returning nothing. The validator abstains because two
readers of the same corpus disagreed, and, less often, because both readers
found the evidence inconclusive. In both cases the pipeline acts as a
disagreement detector and reports its own uncertainty; the price is coverage.

\subsection{Evidence acquisition}

Table~\ref{tab:retrieval} reports what independent retrieval actually
bought. Recall@$k$ measures how often the gold rationale documents appear in
the retrieved set; overlap measures how much of $\Done$ was already in
$\Dzero$; unique yield measures how often retrieval found a relevant
document the original citations missed.

These numbers are unflattering to the hypothesis that independent retrieval
should help. Retrieval finds the annotated documents
most of the time (recall@$k$ = \retrievalRecall{} over the
\retrievalNAnnotated{} claims that have annotated evidence), but every
annotated document it finds was also cited by the report: the unique yield
is \retrievalUnique{}. The limit is in the benchmark, not in the retriever.
In SciFact the cited document set contains the annotated
document set, so a retrieval system that searches the same corpus cannot
find \emph{new gold evidence}; it can only add unannotated context, and
\retrievalUnjudged{}\% of what it returns is unjudged. The independent arm
therefore cannot repair a wrong citation on this corpus, because a wrong
citation is, by construction, a document without a rationale. More retrieval
cannot resolve the D0/D1 conflict, and this property bounds every claim in
this paper.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Evidence acquisition for the independent retrieval arm on the
development sample. Recall@$k$ is over claims that have at least one gold
rationale document; overlap is the mean fraction of retrieved documents
that were also cited by the report.}
\label{tab:retrieval}
\input{paper/tables/t5_retrieval}
\end{table}

\subsection{Calibration, selective use, and cost}

Because the judge emits labels but no probabilities, we report two things.
First, calibration of the one condition that verbalises confidence (B1): a
single temperature fitted on the calibration split, giving Brier score, NLL,
and ECE on the development split (Table~\ref{tab:calibration} and
Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}). Second, a selective-use analysis that does
not require probabilities: accepting a claim only when the two evidence
scopes agree, and measuring error among accepted claims as a function of
coverage. Figure~\ref{fig:riskcoverage} shows the result for both families.
The disagreement-based acceptance rule reaches low error at moderate
coverage, which is the usable form of the system's conservatism.

Table~\ref{tab:cost} reports model calls, measured tokens per call, and
latency for the Luna family. V issues three calls per claim against B2's two,
because it runs a sealed reader, a claim-visible judge, and a citation
auditor. A B2 call measures about \lunadevBTwoTokensPerCall{} tokens and a V
call about \lunadevVTokensPerCall{}, so V's three calls per claim cost roughly
six times B2's two (Figure~\ref{fig:accuracycost} plots quality against
per-call prompt size). The MiniMax family's cost is not in the table: its harness
prepends a fixed agent preamble to every request, so a per-call figure would
measure the harness more than the task, and the endpoint that served the
model was withdrawn before the probe could be run. The call ratio does carry
over, because the three stages are the same three stages. In exchange for
that cost V produces two scoped judgments instead of one. A reader-facing
deployment that only needs a single verdict is better served by B2; the value
of V is that its two scopes are separately auditable.

\subsection{Case studies}
\label{sec:results-cases}

The case records show how the aggregate errors arise. Table~\ref{tab:cases}
in Appendix~\ref{app:cases} records three rows selected deterministically from
the saved predictions: one where the two evidence scopes disagreed, one where
both scopes were unsure and the validator lost a claim the baseline got right,
and one where the baseline endorsed a claim the gold does not support. The
second row shows the cost most directly: the two readers agreed that the
evidence was inconclusive, the gold annotation says the claim is supported, and
no amount of staging recovers it. That is the coverage cost on a single claim.

The dominant class is scope conflict: \lunadevVconflictErrors{} of V's
\lunadevVerrors{} development errors and \lunaheldVconflictErrors{} of its
\lunaheldVerrors{} held-out errors sit on claims where the scopes disagreed,
and V abstains on every one by construction. Execution failures are counted
separately as an execution status: the development run recovered all of them
by retry, and the held-out run, which does not retry, lost
\lunaheldVfailclosed{} of 300 claims to them. We also read a sample of the
\emph{successful} rows, because a system can be accidentally right: several V
successes are cases where the \Dzero{} citation failed to support the claim
while \Done{} supplied better evidence.

\section{Discussion}

\emph{Independent retrieval is not sufficient.} In both model families on
the development sample, and again for the Luna family under the freeze, the
staged validator did not significantly reduce false endorsement relative to
a baseline that already read the original citations. The 95\% interval on
the primary comparison includes zero in all three comparisons we ran.

\emph{Staging trades recall for precision.} The sealed reader makes the
system conservative: it endorses less, and what it endorses is right more
often. Reported as F1 this is a regression; reported as a
precision--coverage curve it is a usable operating point. Both reports are
needed, and readers of verification papers should demand both.

\emph{The main obstacle is disagreement between scopes, not missing
evidence.} Most underdetermined verdicts come from two readers of the same
corpus reaching different conclusions, not from an empty retrieval pool.
Improving retrieval alone will not fix this. A better decision procedure for
the conflict case would help, for example evidence chain evaluation
\citep{yang2026calibratedselective}, scope-matched adjudication, or explicit
conflict reporting to the reader.

We can say nothing about human benefit. Explanations exist in the design,
and prior work shows that explanations and confidence interact with human
calibration \citep{zhang2020trustcalibration}, but we ran no user study.
Appendix~\ref{app:human-study} gives the protocol so that the study can be run
without redesigning it.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{No human annotation.} SciFact's three-way gold cannot score
    the four-way distinction; the unaddressed/underdetermined split is
    descriptive. Every number here is a number about label agreement with a
    crowd-sourced benchmark, not about scientific truth.
  \item \textbf{One corpus, one domain.} Biomedical abstracts, English
    only, abstract-level text. Claims that require full-text methods,
    figures, or supplementary material are out of scope, and the corpus
    bounds every support claim we make.
  \item \textbf{Supplied claims, not generated reports.} The design includes a
    proposer that turns a report into atomic claims, but the evaluation
    scores crowd-sourced SciFact claims, not claims proposed from
    agent-written research reports. A multi-hop agentic track with human
    reference inventories and adjudicated annotation was planned and not
    run, so the results speak to checking a claim whose evidence set is
    given, not to end-to-end report verification.
  \item \textbf{Abstract-level evidence.} Retrieval and reading operate on
    abstracts. Some claims are not decidable from an abstract, which
    should appear as unaddressed but may be read as underdetermined.
  \item \textbf{Model families are not matched.} The two families differ in
    size, training, and harness. The transfer result is about the
    \emph{direction} of the effect, not its magnitude, and the second
    family's harness preamble is included in every request, so its token
    counts are not comparable with the Luna family's.
  \item \textbf{The cross-model sweep is descriptive.} The thirty-claim
    subset is balanced by gold label and frozen before any model was run, but
    it is too small to resolve a false-endorsement difference of one
    percentage point; most paired intervals collapse to zero. It supports a
    statement about the direction of the shift across models, not about its
    size, and it does not reproduce the SUPPORT-recall gap measured on the
    full sample.
  \item \textbf{The MiniMax family's matrix is incomplete.} Its B3 condition
    stopped partway through the sample and its B0, O and calibration
    conditions never ran, because the free endpoint that served the model was
    withdrawn and the remaining requests return a model-unavailable error. The
    MiniMax family therefore corroborates the preregistered V-versus-B2
    contrast and the class breakdown, not the full factorial, and we report
    its missing rows as absent rather than imputing them.
  \item \textbf{One frozen held-out run.} The held-out sample was run once
    under the freeze record, so its interval is a single-run estimate and
    the two families were not both run on it.
  \item \textbf{No matched-budget control was run.} V spends several times
    the tokens of B2, so compute is a live rival explanation for part of the
    F1 gap. The planned control repeats B2's comparison step at $k$ samples
    and votes, matching V's token budget; it is the first experiment we would
    run next. We report the gap with that caveat rather than claiming it is
    explained.
  \item \textbf{Retrieval is BM25 only.} Dense retrieval and
    reciprocal-rank fusion were prepared but not enabled in the product path.
    A stronger retriever could change the D0/D1 overlap numbers.
  \item \textbf{No user study.} See RQ3 and Appendix~\ref{app:human-study}.
\end{itemize}

\section{Ethics and Broader Impact}

The task is interpreting published abstracts, not giving medical advice, and
the system is evaluated only on a frozen research corpus. The rendered
output is a label, a rationale, and a search scope; it is not a clinical
recommendation and the interface says so.

The failure mode we measured is endorsement without evidence. Our system
reduces that risk by abstaining, but abstention has its own risk: a reader
who sees an abstention may infer that the claim is false, which would be a
new error. We therefore keep the scientific verdict (``underdetermined'')
separate from the system action (``defer to a reviewer''), and we recommend
that any deployment display them separately.

The agent harness used for the MiniMax family and for the open-weight rows
of the sweep is an interactive coding agent runtime; a research run inside it
inherits that runtime's permissions and preamble. We ran it with a fixed
preamble, a fixed corpus, and no tool-enabled tasks. The model itself was withdrawn from its free endpoint
during the study, which is why the MiniMax family's matrix is partial; we
report the conditions that completed and do not fill the rest by
substitution.

\section{Conclusion}

We built a staged, evidence-first validator for scientific claims: a sealed
reader, a claim-visible judge over four labels, a citation auditor over the
original references, and a reconciler that reports two evidence scopes
separately, with fail-closed execution semantics throughout. Against a strong
same-evidence baseline, on a frozen corpus, with locked splits, a
preregistered primary comparison, and two model families, the validator did
not significantly reduce false endorsement. It became a conservative checker
whose errors come mostly from disagreement between two readers of the same
literature, and the same direction appears when the pairing is repeated across
the wider set of models we could run: contradictions are withheld, endorsements
are not gained. We report that as a negative result, with the mechanism, the
cost, and the artifact needed to re-run it. The next step is a better
decision procedure for scope disagreement.

\appendix

\section{Prompts and output contracts}
\label{app:prompts}

The prompts are versioned files under \texttt{prompts/}; the run sidecar
records each file's SHA-256 and the bundle hash. The contracts are:

\begin{quote}
\small
\textbf{Reader (claim-blind).} Input: a neutral question and a list of
passages with identifiers. Output: \texttt{\{"answer": str,
"cited\_doc\_ids": [int]\}}. The reader is not shown the claim, the asserted
answer, the report, or any gold rationale.

\textbf{Judge (claim-visible).} Input: the atomic claim, the sealed reader
record, and the passages. Output: \texttt{\{"label": one of supported,
contradicted, unaddressed, underdetermined; "rationale\_codes": [str];
"cited\_span\_ids": [str]; "uncertainty\_reasons": [str]\}}.

\textbf{Citation auditor (D0 only).} Input: the atomic claim and the
original cited passages. Output: the judge contract plus
\texttt{\{"citations": [\{"span\_id": str, "adequacy": adequate |
inadequate | unverifiable, "defects": [str]\}]\}}.

\textbf{Compare (B2).} Input: the claim, the neutral question, and the
sealed reader record. Output: \texttt{\{"label": SUPPORT | REFUTE | NEI,
"rationale": str\}}.
\end{quote}

The exact text of every prompt, and the parser that enforces each contract,
are in the repository. The parsers reject an out-of-set label, a cited
identifier that was not supplied, and a missing mandatory field; each
rejection produces a failed execution status rather than a repaired label.

\section{Metric definitions}
\label{app:metrics}

Let $S$ be the set of scored claims, $g_i \in \{\textsc{support},
\textsc{refute}, \textsc{nei}\}$ the gold label, and $p_i$ the predicted
label. The endorsement class is $E=\textsc{support}$.

\begin{align}
\mathrm{FE}_{\text{gold}} &= \frac{|\{i : p_i = E,\ g_i \neq E\}|}{|\{i : g_i \neq E\}|}
&\mathrm{FE}_{\text{pred}} &= \frac{|\{i : p_i = E,\ g_i \neq E\}|}{|\{i : p_i = E\}|}
\end{align}

Micro-F1 pools the confusion matrix over the three classes; macro-F1 averages
the three per-class F1 values. Coverage is $|\{i : i \text{ produced a scored
prediction}\}| / |S|$. Latency is the median and 95th percentile of the
per-call round-trip time recorded by the client; tokens are the sum of
prompt and completion tokens reported by the endpoint. The paired bootstrap
resamples cited-document families with replacement (2000 resamples) and
reports a percentile interval over the resampled difference; a claim enters
the comparison only if every compared method produced an execution-ok,
gold-labelled row for it, and dropped claims are counted and reported.

\section{Calibration details}
\label{app:calibration}

One temperature is fitted on the calibration split by minimising multiclass
negative log-likelihood over the class scores of the one condition that
verbalises confidence. No parameter is fitted on development or held-out
data. Multiclass Brier score is the mean over claims of
$\sum_k (p_k - \mathbb{1}[k=y])^2$; ECE uses ten equal-width bins on the
predicted probability of the argmax class. The fitted parameters, the class
counts, and the raw-versus-calibrated comparison are in the repository. We
report that numerical calibration is validated only for the condition that
emits scores; for the staged validator, which emits labels only, we report
the disagreement-based selective-use analysis instead and state that its
numerical calibration is unvalidated.

\section{Protocol for the deferred human study}
\label{app:human-study}

No participant was recruited and no ethics review was obtained, so this
paper makes no claim about human benefit. The protocol is recorded here so it
can be executed without redesign and so that the absence of results is
explicit.

\paragraph{Design.} Thirty non-expert adults (a feasible range of 24--36),
plus four to six pilot participants, would each see twelve short,
expert-reviewed items that retain the scientific qualifiers and span
supported, contradicted, and unresolved evidence. Each participant sees each
item once. Condition assignment is counterbalanced across participants so
that item difficulty is not confounded with interface condition:
(A) conclusion plus original citations; (B) A plus the validator verdict and
its uncertainty; (C) B plus the evidence-linked explanation. Conditions B
and C must use the same system verdict and confidence. Four items per
condition per participant, with randomised order and recorded assignment.

\paragraph{Outcomes.} An initial 0--100 judgement that the conclusion is
adequately supported, the same judgement after the assigned interface, a
four-way evidence-status choice, one comprehension question, a use-or-defer
decision, and response time. Expert gold support is defined as
\emph{supported} versus \emph{not established}; ``not established'' is not
described to participants as factual falsity. The primary exploratory
outcome is the post-interface Brier score for evidence support comparing C
with B while adjusting for pre-interface belief and item effects; secondary
outcomes are appropriate acceptance of supported claims, rejection or
deferral of unsupported claims, four-way accuracy, and overreliance when the
validator is wrong. Naturally incorrect validator outputs are included in a
prespecified error stratum, reported separately from natural error prevalence;
any intentionally manipulated advice would require ethics review and
debriefing.

\paragraph{Analysis.} A mixed-effects model with participant and item random
effects if the sample supports it, otherwise participant-level paired
summaries with explicit limits on item generalisation. Responses are not
treated as independent participants. The study is exploratory unless a
prospective power analysis supports stronger claims.

\section{Reproduction}
\label{app:repro}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Install the package and its development extras, and verify the
    pinned corpus hash (\path{data/pins/scifact/}).
  \item Start the model endpoint. For the Luna family, set
    \texttt{OPENAI\_API\_KEY} and \texttt{OPENAI\_MODEL}. For the second
    family, start a local agent server and the loopback bridge in
    \path{tools/opencode_bridge.py}, then pass
    \texttt{-{}-base-url} and \texttt{-{}-model-id} to the runners.
  \item Run the conditions on the development sample
    (\path{scripts/run_api_dev300.sh} for the Luna family,
    \path{scripts/run_minimax_dev300.sh} for the MiniMax family, which also
    shows the bridge setup). The MiniMax family's registered conditions are
    the three that completed; its remaining conditions returned a
    model-unavailable error, as noted in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}.
  \item Run the held-out sample once with \texttt{-{}-frozen-final}; the
    runner refuses to start unless the model, prompt, configuration, and
    corpus hashes match \path{docs/freeze.json}.
  \item Reproduce the cross-model sweep with
    \path{scripts/make_sweep_sample.py} (builds the frozen thirty-claim
    subset from the development manifest and the pinned gold release) and
    \path{scripts/run_model_sweep.sh} (runs B2 and V for each registered
    model, resumably, and stops the closed-weight models at a spend cap).
  \item Regenerate every table and figure
    (\path{scripts/paper/make_tables.py},
    \path{scripts/paper/make_figures.py}) and rebuild the PDF
    (\path{scripts/paper/build_pdf.sh}).
\end{enumerate}

Every number in this paper is read from the generated LaTeX fragments under
\path{paper/tables/}, which are produced from the scored metric JSON files
under \path{docs/paper-assets/tables/}. The prose macros in
\path{paper/tables/macros.tex} are generated by the same script, so a
number in the text cannot drift from the artifact.
